intro:
Today began with one final adventure through Slovenia, and what an adventure it turned out to be.

Leaving Kamnik, I headed toward the Soča Valley and Napoleon’s Bridge. What looked like a beautiful scenic drive quickly became one of the most nerve-racking experiences of the trip.

The roads grew narrower, the curves tighter, and the descent through the mountains seemed endless. With wet pavement, sharp turns, and an unfamiliar Volvo XC90 that already felt enormous on these European roads, I found myself concentrating on every inch of the journey.

If Day 2 had been a 10 out of 10 for driving stress, this morning was easily a 15.

And yet, the scenery was absolutely beautiful.

Slovenia’s mountains reminded me of the Appalachian Mountains back home, but there was something distinctly different about them. Everything felt closer and more intimate. The mountains rose immediately beside the road, the valleys were narrow, and small homes dotted the slopes among the changing autumn colors.

In the Appalachians, you feel like you’re driving through the mountains. Here in Slovenia, you feel like you’re part of them.

Unfortunately, I was so focused on navigating the road that I couldn’t fully appreciate everything around me.

By the time I reached the bottom of that mountain descent, I was more than ready for a little breathing room.


My final destination before leaving Slovenia was Napoleon’s Bridge, near Kobarid, in the beautiful Soča Valley.

The bridge and its surrounding landscape offered one last opportunity to experience the natural beauty that had made Slovenia such a memorable part of this journey.

The mountains, the river, and the dramatic terrain were a reminder of just how much this small country has to offer.

Slovenia had certainly challenged me behind the wheel, but it had also surprised me with its beauty.

And with that, it was time to say goodbye to Slovenia and make my way into Italy.


Venice was next.

After the morning’s mountain adventure, I was looking forward to trading winding roads for canals and historic streets.

Getting into Venice was an experience of its own. Once the car was parked, I made my way into the city using the People Mover and continued on foot toward its famous landmarks.

Walking through Venice was interesting. There were narrow streets, bridges, canals, and beautiful old buildings around nearly every corner.

Eventually, I made my way to St. Mark’s Square and the Bridge of Sighs.

Seeing these places in person was nice, and I appreciated the history and architecture. But I wouldn’t say they were necessarily the highlight of my visit.

That came a little later.

For the return journey, I boarded a water bus along the Grand Canal.

And that changed everything.

As the boat made its way through Venice, the afternoon sunlight illuminated the colorful buildings lining the canal. The reflections danced across the water, and the entire city seemed to come alive.

From the boat, I could finally take in Venice from a completely different perspective.

The architecture, the waterways, the boats passing by, and the sunlight shining down on everything made for an absolutely beautiful experience.

It was easily my favorite part of Venice.

Looking back, I don’t feel like I missed anything by keeping my visit relatively short. I saw the places I wanted to see, wandered through the city, and experienced the Grand Canal in a way that brought the whole visit together.

It felt complete.

And there was something fitting about that final boat ride. The wind and cooler air almost felt like a preview of what was still ahead.

Because while Venice had been today’s adventure, the mountains were calling again.

The Dolomites were waiting.


With Venice behind me, it was time to continue toward Brescia.

After several days of moving between countries, visiting branch offices, exploring unfamiliar cities, and navigating some unforgettable roads, Brescia would become my home base for the next part of the journey.

And after today’s adventures, the thought of settling into one place for a little while sounded pretty wonderful.

For dinner, I decided to embrace the local cuisine and try casonsei, a traditional Brescian stuffed pasta. It seemed only fitting that my first evening in Brescia would include a dish that the region is known for.

After a day filled with mountain roads, Venetian canals, and plenty of unexpected moments, sitting down to a traditional Italian meal was a welcome change of pace.

From the mountains of Slovenia to the canals of Venice, today had been another day of contrasts.

Some moments tested my nerves. Others simply took my breath away.

And sometimes, the most memorable part of a place isn’t necessarily its most famous landmark.

Sometimes, it’s a simple boat ride in the afternoon sunshine that makes the entire experience worthwhile.
